items.prompt: State the term for a sequence of nucleotides that forms part of a DNA molecule and codes for a polypeptide.
items.canonical_answer: The term is gene: a gene is a sequence of nucleotides, forming part of a DNA molecule, that codes for a polypeptide.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the term gene, defined by the key words a sequence of nucleotides that is part of a DNA molecule and codes for a polypeptide. The definition names the polypeptide as the product, not the gene itself.

items.prompt: State what is meant by the term degenerate when it is used of the genetic code.
items.canonical_answer: Degenerate means that most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the key words, more than one codon for the same amino acid. A statement that one codon codes for several amino acids is the reverse and earns no mark; this term means several codons, one amino acid.
items.provenance: Authored for 8223 topic 3.2.2 from its claim ledger. Unverified.
objective_titles: state the features of the genetic code

items.prompt: A learner says: "One base codes for one amino acid, so a stretch of 300 bases, all of which code for amino acids, makes a polypeptide of 300 amino acids." Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is the idea that one base codes for one amino acid. In fact the code is a triplet: three bases code for one amino acid. The 300 bases therefore make 300 ÷ 3 = 100 codons, so a polypeptide of 100 amino acids. The test is to ask how many bases code for one amino acid; the answer is three.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, one base for one amino acid (1); the correct idea, three bases for one amino acid, with the working 300 ÷ 3 = 100 amino acids or the test question (1).
The card is a discrimination between one base and three bases per amino acid, not a repeat of the definition of a codon.
items.provenance: Authored for 8223 topic 3.2.2 from its claim ledger. Unverified.
objective_titles: state the features of the genetic code

items.prompt: Describe, in order, how the information in a gene is used to make a polypeptide in a cell with a nucleus.
items.canonical_answer: First, in transcription, the DNA of the gene unwinds and RNA nucleotides pair with the template strand to make mRNA, which leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore. Then, in translation, the mRNA binds to a ribosome in the cytoplasm and tRNA molecules, each with an anticodon complementary to a codon, bring amino acids in the order of the codons. Finally the ribosome joins the amino acids with peptide bonds until a stop codon releases the polypeptide.
marking_guidance: 3 marks, one for each stage in the correct order: transcription makes mRNA from the template strand in the nucleus (1); the mRNA binds to a ribosome and tRNA anticodons pair with codons to bring the amino acids (1); the amino acids are joined in the order of the codons until a stop codon, giving the polypeptide (1).
The sequence is the point: translation described before transcription earns no mark. The result, a polypeptide with its amino acids in the order the gene codes for, is the end of the answer.

items.prompt: Describe how a tRNA molecule makes sure that the correct amino acid is added at a codon on the mRNA.
items.canonical_answer: Each tRNA carries one particular amino acid at one end and has an anticodon at the other end. The anticodon is complementary to a codon, so it pairs with that codon by base pairing and not with others. The amino acid brought is therefore the one that the codon codes for.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: how the anticodon pairs with the codon by complementary bases (1); because the amino acid at the other end is the one that the codon codes for, the correct amino acid arrives (1).
A learner who writes that the anticodon is the same as the codon has the mechanism wrong and earns neither mark.

items.prompt: A ribosome in a marula leaf cell is reading the mRNA codon GAG. Explain why a tRNA with the anticodon CUC binds at this codon and which amino acid it brings. The codon GAG codes for glutamic acid.
items.canonical_answer: The anticodon CUC is complementary to the codon GAG: C pairs with G, U pairs with A and C pairs with G. So it can pair with the codon, whereas a tRNA with the anticodon GAG would have the same bases as the codon and could not pair with it. The tRNA brings glutamic acid, because that is the amino acid the codon codes for.
marking_guidance: 2 marks tied to the given codon: CUC is complementary to GAG, base by base, so it can pair (1); the tRNA brings glutamic acid because that is what GAG codes for (1).
In this case the answer must use the bases in the situation given; a general statement about anticodons earns no mark.

items.prompt: A learner says: "In transcription the DNA is copied, so the mRNA has the same base sequence as the template strand." Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is saying that the mRNA is a copy of the template strand. In fact the mRNA is built from RNA nucleotides that pair with the template strand, so it is complementary to it: the template triplet TAC gives the codon AUG, and U takes the place of T. The test is to ask what the product is, DNA, RNA or protein, and what it is built from. In transcription the product is RNA, built from RNA nucleotides.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, that the mRNA has the same sequence as the template strand, when it is complementary to it and built from RNA nucleotides (1); the correct idea with an example such as TAC giving AUG, or the test of product and building material (1).
The card discriminates complementary from copy; a repeat of the definition of transcription alone earns neither mark.

items.prompt:
A table lists, for the first three codons of an mRNA, the tRNA that binds to each codon. The data are our own.

|---|---|---|
| AUG | UAC | methionine |
| ACU | UGA | threonine |
| CCU | GGA | proline |

Describe what the table shows about how each anticodon is related to its codon.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows that each anticodon is complementary to its codon, base by base: A in the codon pairs with U in the anticodon, U with A, C with G and G with C. Each row means that the anticodon pairs with its codon and the amino acid carried is the one the codon codes for.
marking_guidance: 2 marks read from the table: each anticodon is complementary to its codon, with a base-pairing example read from a row (1); the amino acid in the row is the one the codon codes for, which means the codon decides the amino acid carried (1).
A reading that says the anticodon is the same as the codon contradicts the data in every row and earns no mark.

items.prompt: State what is meant by a gene mutation.
items.canonical_answer: A gene mutation is a change in the sequence of nucleotides (bases) in a gene, which may result in an altered polypeptide.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the key words, a change in the sequence of nucleotides (or bases) in a gene. The term means a change to the gene, not to the polypeptide; a change in the number of whole chromosomes does not answer this.

items.prompt: State what is meant by a substitution mutation.
items.canonical_answer: A substitution mutation is a gene mutation in which one base pair is replaced by a different base pair.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the key words, one base pair replaced by a different base pair. The term means a replacement, so an added or lost base pair is an insertion or deletion and does not earn the mark.

items.prompt: Explain how the deletion of one base from the middle of a gene can change the amino acids that come after the deletion.
items.canonical_answer: The codons are read in threes from a fixed start. If one base is deleted, the groups of three after the deletion move along by one base, so each later codon is made of a different set of three bases. This frameshift generally changes the amino acids that come after that point, and may bring in a stop codon early.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the codons are read in threes, so removing one base shifts the reading frame (1); which means each codon after the deletion is a different set of three bases, so the later amino acids generally change (1).
A statement that only one amino acid changes describes a substitution, not this mechanism, and earns no mark.

items.prompt: In a gene fragment from a tsamma melon, the normal allele gives the mRNA codons AUG ACU CCU GAG AAG UUU UAA, where UAA is a stop codon. In a mutant allele the fifth codon is UAG instead of AAG, and UAG is also a stop codon. Explain the effect of this mutation on the polypeptide.
items.canonical_answer: In the mutant the fifth codon UAG is a stop codon, so translation ends there. The polypeptide has only the four amino acids coded by the first four codons, not the six of the normal polypeptide, because the amino acids after the stop codon are never added. It is a nonsense substitution and the shorter polypeptide is unlikely to work.
marking_guidance: 2 marks tied to the information given: UAG is a stop codon, so translation ends at the fifth codon (1); because of this the polypeptide has four amino acids instead of six, so it is shorter (1).
In this case the answer must use the codons given, and the numbers four and six are the evidence; a general statement about mutation earns no mark.

items.prompt:
A table gives the mRNA codons for the third codon of the normal gene and of two mutant alleles of a gene. All other codons are the same. The data are our own. The codons GAG and GAA both code for glutamic acid (Glu) and GUG codes for valine (Val).

| Allele | Third codon |
|---|---|
| Normal | GAG |
| Mutant 1 | GAA |
| Mutant 2 | GUG |

Describe what the table shows about the effect of each mutation on the polypeptide.
items.canonical_answer: Mutant 1 has GAA in place of GAG, and both code for Glu, so the polypeptide is unchanged, because the code is degenerate. Mutant 2 has GUG in place of GAG, which means the third amino acid is Val and not Glu, so the polypeptide has one amino acid different.
marking_guidance: 2 marks read from the data: Mutant 1 shows no change to the polypeptide because both codons code for Glu (1); Mutant 2 shows one amino acid changed, Glu replaced by Val (1).

Both mutants are substitutions of one base; the table means the effect depends on whether the new codon codes for the same amino acid. A statement that both mutants change the polypeptide earns no mark.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "The codon GUG is found at the end of the tRNA molecule, and it is the amino acid valine." Explain the errors.
items.canonical_answer: The error is that a codon, an anticodon and an amino acid are being treated as one thing. In fact GUG is a codon, which sits on the mRNA, not on the tRNA. The tRNA has the complementary anticodon CAC at one end, and the amino acid valine is a separate molecule carried at the other end of the tRNA. The test is to ask which one sits on mRNA, which on tRNA, and which is carried.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, that the codon is not on the tRNA but on the mRNA, and the tRNA has the complementary anticodon CAC (1); the correct idea that the amino acid is carried at the other end of the tRNA and is not a set of bases (1).
The card discriminates the three terms, using the test, and does not repeat a definition of one of them.

items.prompt:
A table gives the template strand for one short stretch of the beta-globin gene, read 3′ to 5′, with the mRNA made 5′ to 3′ in the HbA and HbS alleles, and the polypeptide stretch that each makes. The data are our own and are simplified.

| Allele | Template strand | Polypeptide stretch |

| HbA | 3′-TGA GGA CTC CTC TTC-5′ | Thr-Pro-Glu-Glu-Lys |
| HbS | 3′-TGA GGA CAC CTC TTC-5′ | Thr-Pro-Val-Glu-Lys |

Describe what the table shows about how the change in the template strand leads to the change in the polypeptide.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows that the third template triplet changes from CTC to CAC. Read 5′ to 3′, the mRNA codon therefore changes from GAG to GUG, so the third amino acid of the stretch (residue 6 of the mature chain) changes from Glu to Val. The other four triplets and amino acids are unchanged, which means one base-pair change gives a change of one amino acid.
marking_guidance: 2 marks read from the table: the third template triplet differs, CTC in HbA and CAC in HbS, a single base (1); this gives a different codon, GAG to GUG, so one amino acid differs, Glu in HbA and Val in HbS, while the others are unchanged (1).
The data show a change of one amino acid in five; an answer that says the whole polypeptide differs earns no mark.

items.prompt: A class is making a model of a short mRNA strand to contrast with a model of DNA. Describe, in order, how to build the RNA model.
items.canonical_answer: First, choose pieces for phosphate and ribose and a different colour for each base A, U, G and C, with no thymine piece. Then join a phosphate, a ribose and a base into each nucleotide and join the nucleotides through the phosphate and sugar into one backbone. The result is a single strand with the bases pointing out, which can be placed beside the two-stranded DNA model to contrast the strands, the sugar and uracil in place of thymine.
marking_guidance: 3 marks, in order: pieces and a colour code chosen with uracil and no thymine (1); each nucleotide built from phosphate, ribose and a base, then joined into one backbone (1); the result is a single strand, compared with the two-stranded DNA model (1).
The order is the point: the strand cannot be joined before the nucleotides are built. Ribose and uracil are the two pieces that make the model RNA and not DNA.

marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason, because mRNA is a single strand and DNA is double stranded. An answer that says it is to save materials is not a reason about the molecule and earns no mark.

items.prompt:
Twelve questions. Choose one option for each.

1. Which statement describes a gene?
A  a sequence of amino acids that forms a protein
B  a sequence of nucleotides that forms part of a DNA molecule and codes for a polypeptide
C  a molecule of mRNA that carries codons to a ribosome
D  a whole chromosome made of DNA and histone proteins

2. How many bases on the mRNA code for a polypeptide of 40 amino acids, not counting any stop codon?
A  40
B  80
C  120
D  160

3. The genetic code is described as degenerate. What does this mean?
A  Each codon codes for more than one amino acid.
B  Most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon.
C  The codons share bases with their neighbours.
D  The codons differ between species.

4. The template strand of a gene reads TAC GGA. What is the mRNA made from it?
A  ATG CCT
B  AUG CCU
C  UAC GGA
D  TAC GGA

5. Where does translation take place?
A  in the nucleus, on the template strand
B  at a nuclear pore
C  at a ribosome in the cytoplasm
D  on a molecule of RNA polymerase

6. The mRNA codon CCU is being read. Which anticodon, written so that it lines up under the codon, pairs with it?
A  CCU
B  GGT
C  GGU
D  GGA

7. Which statement about a tRNA molecule is correct?
A  It has an anticodon at one end and carries an amino acid at the other end.
B  It has a codon at one end and carries an amino acid at the other end.
C  It carries an amino acid at the same end as the anticodon.
D  Its anticodon is complementary to the template strand and not to the codon.

8. What joins the amino acids together during translation?
A  hydrogen bonds between the anticodons
B  hydrogen bonds between the amino acids
C  ester bonds made by RNA polymerase
D  peptide bonds made at the ribosome

9. One base is deleted from the middle of a gene. What is the effect on the polypeptide?
A  The codons after the deletion are read in a different frame, so the amino acids after it generally change.
B  Only one amino acid changes and the rest are the same.
C  The polypeptide is unchanged because the code is degenerate.
D  The polypeptide has one extra amino acid and the rest are the same.

10. A mutation changes the mRNA codon GAG to GAA. Both codons code for glutamic acid. What is the effect on the polypeptide?
A  One amino acid is changed.
B  The polypeptide is shortened.
C  The polypeptide is unchanged, because the code is degenerate.
D  The reading frame is shifted.

11. A mutation changes the mRNA codon AAG to UAG, a stop codon. What is the effect on the polypeptide?
A  It has the same amino acids.
B  It is shorter, because translation stops at the changed codon.
C  One amino acid is replaced by another and the length is the same.
D  It is longer, because a stop codon adds amino acids.

12. Which statement describes the difference between the HbA and HbS alleles of the beta-globin gene?
A  A base pair is deleted, which causes a frameshift.
B  A whole codon is inserted, so an amino acid is added.
C  One base pair is substituted, which changes one codon so that valine replaces glutamic acid.
D  The tRNA anticodon is different, which changes the mRNA.
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 B, 2 C, 3 B, 4 B, 5 C, 6 D, 7 A, 8 D, 9 A, 10 C, 11 B, 12 C.
1. A gene is a sequence of nucleotides that is part of DNA and codes for a polypeptide (B). A describes the polypeptide, which is the product, not the gene; C is mRNA, which is made from the gene; D is a whole chromosome, which carries many genes.
2. Each amino acid needs a codon of three bases, so 40 × 3 = 120 (C). A is an error from one base per amino acid; B comes from two bases per amino acid; D comes from using the four kinds of base as the number per amino acid.
3. Degenerate means that most amino acids have more than one codon (B). A reverses the relation, with one codon for many amino acids; C describes an overlapping code; D describes a code that is not universal.
4. The mRNA is complementary to the template strand and built from RNA nucleotides, so TAC gives AUG and GGA gives CCU (B). A uses T, which is a DNA base, in the RNA; C copies the template with U for T instead of pairing; D copies the template exactly.
5. Translation takes place at a ribosome in the cytoplasm (C). A places it in the nucleus, where transcription happens; B names the place the mRNA leaves the nucleus; D confuses it with the enzyme that makes mRNA.
6. The anticodon is complementary to the codon: C pairs with G and U pairs with A, so CCU needs GGA (D). A is the codon itself, an error from not pairing; B uses T, a DNA base, in an RNA anticodon; C pairs U with U, which is not a base pair.
7. A tRNA has the anticodon at one end and carries an amino acid at the other end (A). B puts a codon on the tRNA, but codons are on mRNA; C puts the amino acid at the anticodon end; D has the anticodon pairing with the template, but it pairs with the codon.
8. The ribosome joins amino acids with peptide bonds (D). A and B give hydrogen bonds, which hold anticodons to codons and do not join amino acids; C gives RNA polymerase a job in translation, but it makes mRNA in transcription.
9. Deleting one base shifts the frame, so later codons are different sets of three bases (A). B describes a substitution; C wrongly applies degeneracy to a frameshift; D describes the insertion of a whole codon.
10. GAA and GAG both code for glutamic acid, so the polypeptide is unchanged (C). A is the error of assuming every substitution changes an amino acid; B would need a stop codon; D would need an insertion or deletion.
11. UAG is a stop codon, so translation ends at that codon and the polypeptide is shorter (B). A is an error from ignoring the stop codon; C describes a missense substitution; D reverses the effect of a stop codon.
12. One base pair is substituted, which changes GAG to GUG, so valine replaces glutamic acid (C). A and B describe a deletion and an insertion, which are different mutations; D puts the change on the tRNA, but the change is in the gene.
marking_guidance: The key: one mark per correct option, twelve marks in all; about half the questions test recall and half test a sequence, a count or a described mutation.

Each distractor is a named error: codon, anticodon and amino acid confused, a DNA base written in RNA, mRNA copied and not made complementary, one base or two bases per amino acid, a deletion treated as a substitution.

items.prompt:
A research student in Windhoek compares the same short stretch of a gene in a normal allele and a mutant allele. These are our own data.

| Allele | mRNA codons, left to right | Amino acids |
|---|---|---|
| Normal | AUG ACU CCU GAG AAG UUU UAA | Met, Thr, Pro, Glu, Lys, Phe, stop |
| Mutant | AUG ACU CCU GUG AAG UUU UAA | Met, Thr, Pro, Val, Lys, Phe, stop |

(a) State the type of mutation that has changed the fourth codon, and the number of base pairs changed. [2]
(b) Explain why the mutant polypeptide is the same length as the normal polypeptide but has a different amino acid. [2]
(c) Describe how the tRNA that brings valine at the mutant codon GUG pairs with the codon. [2]
(d) Suggest why this change may alter the way the protein works. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) A substitution; one base pair.
(b) Only one codon has changed, from GAG to GUG, and no base pair has been added or removed, so the reading frame is the same and there are still six codons before the stop codon, giving six amino acids. GUG codes for valine and GAG codes for glutamic acid, so the fourth amino acid is different.
(c) The tRNA has the anticodon CAC at one end, which is complementary to the codon GUG, so the bases pair (C with G, A with U, C with G). The amino acid valine is carried at the other end of the tRNA.
(d) The new amino acid may have a different side chain from glutamic acid, for example it may have no charge, so the way the polypeptide folds may change. The shape of the protein may then change, so its function may change.
marking_guidance: Marks and points: (a) 1 mark for substitution, 1 mark for one base pair; (b) 2 marks from three points: one codon changed with no base pair added or removed so the frame is the same, the number of codons is unchanged, GUG codes for valine and GAG for glutamic acid; (c) 2 marks from three points: anticodon CAC, complementary to the codon by base pairing, valine carried at the other end; (d) 2 marks from three points: a different amino acid may have a different side chain, the folding may change, so the shape and function may change.

Parts (a) and (c) credit AO A (4 marks); parts (b) and (d) credit AO B (4 marks). The reason in (b) must use the sequences in the table because the data given are the evidence; the term in (a) is the name of the mutation.
